title: SSE prefetch window oscillation — repro notes & commands
content:
Quick summary:
I’m tracking a recurring flake where SSE responses from the hosted runtime intermittently produce partial/short frames and then stall for ~100-500ms before the remaining chunks arrive. Under moderate QPS this oscillation pattern becomes periodic (bursty), causing clients to interpret it as repeated reconnects or truncated events. Suspect prefetch/pipeline window math in the sender combined with KV-cache flushes and the continuous-batching loop.

Observed symptoms (client-side):
- Client receives an event header and then a ~1–4 chunk partial payload, then no data for 120–480ms, then the rest of payload arrives in one lump.
- Some clients report "unexpected EOF while parsing event" if timeout < stall gap.
- Trace IDs show chunks leaving different worker threads (sometimes workerA then workerB) with a small timestamp gap.
- Under higher concurrency, the oscillation period shortens and amplitude increases.

Minimal repro (local, single-host):
1) Start a debug build of runtime with verbose streaming logs enabled (LOG_STREAM=debug).
2) Launch a small model handler that emits a 2.5KB event in multiple writes (simulate generation flush): it writes 512 bytes, flush, then writes remainder after a short sleep.
3) Hammer the endpoint with 40 concurrent clients sending a single stream request each, 2 rps per client.

Commands I used to reproduce: (change host/port as needed)

# 1) Simple curl-based SSE consumer to watch raw chunks
curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
  -H "X-Request-ID: repro-001" \
  http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate

# 2) Python streaming reader script (requests) — logs inter-chunk timing
python - <<'PY'
import requests, time
r = requests.get('http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate', headers={'Accept':'text/event-stream','X-Request-ID':'repro-py'}, stream=True, timeout=10)
start = time.time()
for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=None):
    now = time.time()
    print(f"+{now-start:.3f}s : got {len(chunk)} bytes")
PY

# 3) wrk-based concurrency burn (Lua script to keep SSE client alive)
# saves us from re-opening connections every time
wrk -t8 -c40 -d30s -s ./scripts/sse_keepopen.lua http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate

# 4) Node fetch loop (browser-like client) to reproduce edge parsing failures
# run with node repro-node.js
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
(async function(){
  const r = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate', {headers:{'Accept':'text/event-stream','X-Request-ID':'repro-node'}});
  const reader = r.body.getReader();
  let last = Date.now();
  while(true){
    const {value, done} = await reader.read();
    if(done) break;
    if(value) console.log(`${Date.now()-last}ms -> ${value.length} bytes`); last = Date.now();
  }
})();

Server-side logs I captured (sanitized):
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.452Z] worker-07 send_frame seq=1024 len=512 flush=true route=streamer-1 xid=abcd1234
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.574Z] worker-02 send_frame seq=1025 len=2048 flush=true route=streamer-1 xid=abcd1234
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.578Z] kvcache evict key=model:prefix:abcd (policy=LRU)
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.590Z] batching-loop drain=8 prefetched=4 window=6
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.603Z] sock-send partial=512 bytes_sent=512 pending=1536 fd=62
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.723Z] sock-send bytes_sent=0 errno=EAGAIN fd=62
- [2026-02-11T14:21:07.992Z] sock-send resume, bytes_sent=1536 fd=62

Interpretation of logs:
- Frames for the same request are being sent by different workers (seq 1024 from worker-07, seq 1025 from worker-02). That implies request routing or continuation tasks may move ownership between threads when prefetch/batching decisions change.
- kvcache eviction coincides with a batching-loop drain/prefetch change before the stall. Possibly eviction triggers a sync or GC that blocks or deprioritizes socket writes for a small amount of time.
- The kernel EAGAIN shows the socket send buffer was temporarily full; resume later after ~400ms. Why did buffer fill? either transient backlog or slow underlying TCP ack pacing. But we see partial writes (512 then pending) rather than holding the entire payload in memory and writing atomically.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Prefetch window miscalculation: when the batching loop adjusts the prefetch window (due to transient load or cache eviction), in-flight buffers for the request get split across workers and flush boundaries, causing interleaved writes and socket buffer pressure.
2) KV cache eviction/GC path takes a global lock or causes context switches that increase write latency, producing backpressure at the socket level.
3) The continuous-batching code yields ownership of a request mid-response (yield/await) and another worker picks up and writes remainder; thread migration + socket buffering leads to ordering/timing gaps.
4) Kernel/TCP scaling: on some nodes send buffer defaults are tiny, causing EAGAIN sooner. Less likely since repro on multiple hosts.

Quick experiments and results:
- Force single-threaded worker: oscillation disappears (strong evidence for cross-worker handoff being relevant).
- Disable KV-cache eviction (make large cache): stalls drop by ~90% but still occasional gaps — suggests eviction amplifies but isn't sole cause.
- Increase socket send buffer (sysctl net.core.wmem_max/wmem_default): marginal improvement.
- Add an explicit per-request write lock so only the owning worker writes until response is finished — almost eliminates the partial-split pattern, but this is heavy-handed and may hurt throughput.

Short-term mitigations for prod rollout:
- Add a short (5ms) write-coalescing hold: when a worker flushes a partial frame and another partial is queued, wait up to N ms to coalesce. This reduces observed stalls but can add latency tail.
- Bypass cross-worker handoff for streaming responses: pin response to initial worker thread while in-flight. (safe fallback)
- Increase default socket send buffer and tune kernel tcp_low_latency flags for streaming nodes.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Re-run with instrumented per-request ownership trace (tag frames with owner-id and stack) and correlate with exact time of kvcache evict events.
- Add metric that counts "ownership handoffs" during active streaming responses. Target: <1% per 10k streams.
- Try a lighter-weight per-request handshake: initial worker marks response critical and other workers must forward frames to original worker rather than write directly. Evaluate overhead.
- Reproduce on dedicated staging with mixed batch sizes (seq len variance) to ensure this isn't specific to our synthetic generator.

Random notes / crumbs I wrote while experimenting:
- saw one case where a TLS renegotiation (client) caused a 300ms stall — unlikely root cause but keep in mind for mutual TLS endpoints.
- interesting correlation between batcher.window==6 and observed period ~410ms — need to instrument window increment/decrement events.
- reproduce script that toggles kvcache pressure: run a tight loop of embedding requests to force eviction while streaming test is running.

Files/scripts referenced in this note:
- scripts/sse_keepopen.lua (wrk script)
- repro/repro-node.js (node consumer above)
- infra/sysctl-tune.sh (ephemeral changes for testing)

If you want to replicate quickly on your laptop:
1) git checkout my/debug-sse-ownership-logs
2) make run-local (starts runtime on :8080)
3) run: wrk -t2 -c10 -d20s -s scripts/sse_keepopen.lua http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/generate
4) tail -f /tmp/runtime-stream.log | grep "send_frame\|kvcache\|sock-send"

If you pick this up, first step is to add the ownership handoff metric and a simple trace to see exact handoff timestamps relative to kvcache ops. I can pair to walk through the tracing bits — Jonah did a good proto for the per-request tagger that we can reuse.

-- Aisha
